questions.title: Incorrect statement about eukaryotic DNA polymerases
questions.question: Regarding DNA polymerases in eukaryotes, one of the following is NOT correct:

options.A: Polymerase α forms a complex with primase that catalyzes synthesis of RNA primers.
options.B: Polymerase β is concerned with DNA repair.
options.C: Polymerase γ is concerned with replication of mitochondrial DNAs.
options.D: Polymerase ε catalyzes removal of RNA primer

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Polymerase α works as a complex with primase, and that primase activity is what synthesises the short RNA primers needed to start replication.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Polymerase β is the small, repair-associated eukaryotic polymerase, active in base excision repair rather than in bulk genome replication.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Polymerase γ is the dedicated mitochondrial DNA polymerase, replicating the mitochondrial genome independently of the nuclear replication machinery.
explanations.D: Correct — this is the false statement being asked for. Removal of RNA primers in eukaryotic replication is carried out by RNase H1 and FEN1 (flap endonuclease 1), not by polymerase ε. Polymerase ε is instead a high-fidelity, proofreading-capable polymerase associated with leading-strand-type synthesis, so crediting it with primer excision is the error that makes this option the one that is NOT correct.

questions.title: Correct statement about lagging-strand elongation
questions.question: Which statement about the elongation of the lagging strand during DNA replication is correct?

options.A: It is synthesized in a 3' --> 5' direction.
options.B: It progresses (grows) toward the replication fork.
options.C: It requires a short RNA primer to proceed.

explanations.A: Incorrect. All DNA synthesis, including the lagging strand's, proceeds 5' to 3'; there is no known DNA polymerase that extends a strand 3' to 5'.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Because synthesis is always 5' to 3' but the lagging-strand template runs the opposite way relative to the fork, the lagging strand is actually built in short pieces that grow away from the fork, not toward it.
explanations.C: Correct. Each Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand needs its own short RNA primer, laid down by primase, before DNA polymerase can extend it — unlike the leading strand, which only needs one primer at the origin. This repeated priming is what makes lagging-strand synthesis discontinuous. It is one of the clearest distinguishing features between leading- and lagging-strand replication.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Continuous synthesis describes the leading strand; the lagging strand is built discontinuously, as a series of separately primed Okazaki fragments later joined by ligase.

questions.title: Cell-cycle phase of DNA replication
questions.question: During which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?

explanations.A: Incorrect. G1 is a growth/preparatory gap phase before replication begins; the cell builds proteins and organelles here but does not yet copy its DNA.
explanations.B: Correct. The S (synthesis) phase of the cell cycle is defined by DNA replication: the entire genome is duplicated once, converting each chromosome from one to two sister chromatids. It sits between the G1 and G2 gap phases, and its completion is checked before the cell is allowed to enter mitosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. G2 is the second gap phase, after replication is complete, during which the cell prepares for mitosis (e.g. further growth and checkpoint control) rather than copying DNA.
explanations.D: Incorrect. M phase is mitosis itself, when the already-duplicated chromosomes are segregated into two daughter cells; no new DNA synthesis occurs here.

questions.title: Role of topoisomerases in eukaryotic replication
questions.question: What is the role of topoisomerases in eukaryotic DNA replication?

options.A: Topoisomerase enzymes cut, uncoil and reseal the double stranded DNA.
options.B: Topoisomerase enzymes bind to the origin of replication sites within double stranded DNA.
options.C: Topoisomerase enzymes open up the double stranded DNA at the replication fork.
options.D: Topoisomerase enzymes join the Okazaki fragments together with phosphodiester bonds.

explanations.A: Correct. Topoisomerases relieve the positive supercoiling that builds up ahead of the advancing replication fork by transiently cutting one or both DNA strands, letting the helix rotate or pass through the break to release torsional strain, and then resealing the cut. This cut-uncoil-reseal cycle is what lets helicase keep unwinding the parental duplex without the DNA snarling on itself. Without topoisomerase activity, the accumulating supercoils would stall the fork.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Binding origins of replication is the role of origin-recognition proteins (e.g. the origin recognition complex), not topoisomerases.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Opening up (unwinding) the double helix at the fork is the job of helicase, which breaks the hydrogen bonds between strands; topoisomerases act ahead of the fork on supercoiling, not on strand separation itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Joining Okazaki fragments with phosphodiester bonds is the role of DNA ligase, a distinct enzyme from topoisomerase.

questions.title: What DNA polymerase activity does not require
questions.question: DNA polymerase activity does not require one of the following:

options.B: A primer with a free 5'-hydroxyl group.
options.D: A primer with a free 3'-hydroxyl group.

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this is required). DNA polymerase reads an existing strand as a template to decide which base to add next, so a template DNA strand is essential.
explanations.B: Correct — this is the one NOT required. DNA polymerase does not need a free 5'-hydroxyl on the primer; it adds new nucleotides onto the primer's free 3'-hydroxyl end, extending the chain in the 5' to 3' direction. A 5'-OH plays no role in the polymerisation reaction itself, which is why this is the requirement that does not actually apply.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this is required). The four deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP) are the actual building blocks incorporated into the new strand.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this is required). DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides onto a free 3'-hydroxyl group; this is the chemical basis of its 5'-to-3' synthesis direction and why it cannot start a chain de novo.

questions.title: Direction of DNA synthesis
questions.question: The direction of DNA synthesis is:

explanations.A: Correct. Every known DNA polymerase adds new nucleotides only onto the free 3'-hydroxyl end of the growing strand, so synthesis always proceeds 5' to 3' with respect to the new strand. This is true for both the leading strand and every Okazaki fragment of the lagging strand, and it holds across prokaryotes and eukaryotes alike.
explanations.B: Incorrect. No DNA polymerase extends a strand 3' to 5'; that would require adding nucleotides onto a 5' end, which the chemistry of the polymerisation reaction does not support.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Synthesis direction is not random — it is fixed by the enzyme's mechanism, which requires a free 3'-OH to extend.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The 5'-to-3' rule is universal across organisms; it is a fundamental property of how DNA polymerases work, not something that varies by species.

questions.title: Synthesis pattern after fork formation
questions.question: After formation of the replication fork:

options.B: One strand is synthesized continuously and the other discontinuously
options.D: RNA primer is required only for the synthesis of one new strand.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Only the lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously; the leading strand is synthesised continuously in one direction from a single primer.
explanations.B: Correct. Because both template strands are antiparallel but DNA polymerase can only extend 5' to 3', one new strand (the leading strand) is built continuously toward the fork, while the other (the lagging strand) is built discontinuously, as a series of Okazaki fragments primed separately and later joined. This asymmetry is called semi-discontinuous replication.
explanations.C: Incorrect. If both strands were synthesised continuously, the lagging strand's template (which runs the 'wrong' way relative to the fork) could not be copied 5' to 3' without discontinuous fragments.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both new strands require RNA priming — the leading strand needs one primer at the origin, and the lagging strand needs a fresh primer for every Okazaki fragment, so priming is not limited to a single strand.

questions.title: True statement about eukaryotic DNA polymerases
questions.question: As regard eukaryotic DNA polymerases:

options.C: Polymerase ε excise RNA primer and fill the gaps.

explanations.A: Incorrect per this source's key. Mitochondrial DNA replication is carried out by polymerase γ, not β — β is the small repair polymerase.
explanations.B: Incorrect per this source's key. This source grades leading-strand assignment as not the credited statement here; textbooks vary on whether δ or ε is emphasised for leading- versus lagging-strand synthesis, but the source's own answer table marks only option D as correct for this item.
explanations.C: Incorrect per this source's key, and consistent with this chapter's own Q2: primer excision in eukaryotic replication is attributed to RNase H1/FEN1, not to polymerase ε acting alone.
explanations.D: Correct. Polymerase α works together with primase as a single complex, and that complex synthesises the short RNA primers that start both leading- and lagging-strand synthesis in eukaryotes. This is the most secure, textbook-uncontested fact among the four options, which is why it is the one the source's key credits.

questions.title: Role of prokaryotic DNA polymerase III
questions.question: In prokaryotes, DNA polymerase III is responsible for:

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Polymerase III does synthesise the leading strand, but it also synthesises the lagging strand, so option A alone is incomplete.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. Polymerase III does synthesise the lagging strand's Okazaki fragments, but it synthesises the leading strand too, so option B alone is incomplete.
explanations.C: Incorrect. DNA repair in prokaryotes is mainly the role of polymerase I (and associated repair enzymes), not the main replicative polymerase III.
explanations.D: Correct. In prokaryotes, a single enzyme, DNA polymerase III holoenzyme, is the main replicative polymerase and synthesises both the leading strand continuously and the lagging strand's Okazaki fragments discontinuously, using two core complexes at the replication fork. This is different from eukaryotes, which use separate polymerases for the two strands.

questions.title: Enzyme that forms the prokaryotic RNA primer
questions.question: Prokaryotic RNA primer is formed by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Polymerase α is a eukaryotic enzyme (paired with its own primase activity); it is not the prokaryotic primer-forming enzyme this question asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. DNA polymerase III is the main prokaryotic replicative polymerase, but it cannot start a new strand de novo — it extends the primer that primase has already laid down.
explanations.C: Correct. Primase is the RNA polymerase-like enzyme that synthesises the short RNA primer needed before any DNA polymerase can begin extending a strand, in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. In bacteria this is the enzyme DnaG, which lays down a fresh primer for each Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand as well as the single primer that starts the leading strand.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Telomerase is a eukaryotic enzyme that extends the ends of linear chromosomes; it plays no role in prokaryotic replication, and prokaryotic chromosomes are typically circular and have no telomeres to maintain.

questions.title: Enzyme not required in DNA repair
questions.question: One of the following is not required in DNA repair:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this is required). An endonuclease makes the internal cut that excises the damaged stretch of DNA, opening the site for repair synthesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this is required). An exonuclease trims away the excised, damaged nucleotides from the cut end before new DNA is synthesised.
explanations.C: Correct. Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling ahead of replication forks and during other processes that unwind large stretches of DNA, but standard excision-repair pathways (base or nucleotide excision repair) do not depend on it — the repair patch is short and does not generate the topological strain that topoisomerase exists to resolve. This makes topoisomerase the enzyme in this list that repair does not require.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this is required). A repair DNA polymerase fills in the gap left after the damaged stretch is excised, using the intact complementary strand as template.

questions.title: Enzyme that removes RNA primers in prokaryotic replication
questions.question: The following enzyme is responsible for removal of RNA primers during prokaryotic replication:

explanations.A: Correct. DNA polymerase I has a 5'-to-3' exonuclease activity that removes the RNA primers left behind by primase, and it simultaneously fills the resulting gaps with DNA using its polymerase activity. This is the classic nick-translation step of prokaryotic replication, occurring immediately before DNA ligase seals the remaining nick. It is a small, repair-capable polymerase distinct from the main replicative polymerase III.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primase is the enzyme that lays down the RNA primer in the first place; it does not remove it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. DNA polymerase III is the main replicative enzyme that extends the primer with new DNA; primer removal is a separate step carried out by polymerase I.
explanations.D: Incorrect. RNase H can degrade RNA within an RNA:DNA hybrid in some organisms, but in the standard prokaryotic replication pathway taught here, primer excision and gap-filling is credited to DNA polymerase I's 5'→3' exonuclease activity.

questions.title: Eukaryote-versus-prokaryote replication difference
questions.question: Eukaryotes differ from prokaryote in mechanism of DNA replication in:

options.A: Use of DNA primer rather than RNA primer
options.B: Different enzyme for synthesis of lagging and leading strand

explanations.A: Incorrect. Both eukaryotes and prokaryotes use a short RNA primer, not a DNA primer, to initiate synthesis; this is not a point of difference between them.
explanations.B: Correct. Prokaryotes use one polymerase, DNA polymerase III, for both the leading and lagging strands. Eukaryotes instead use separate polymerases (classically ε- and δ-associated activities) for the two strands. This division of labour between two different enzymes is a genuine mechanistic difference between the two replication systems.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Both eukaryotic and prokaryotic replication are semi-discontinuous (continuous leading strand, discontinuous lagging strand); neither system is purely discontinuous on both strands.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Replication is semi-discontinuous (not unidirectional) in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes at each fork; this option also misstates the comparison being drawn.

questions.title: Where Okazaki fragments occur and how they are joined
questions.question: Okazaki fragments occur on the _________ and are bonded together by _________.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The leading strand is synthesised as one continuous piece, not as separate fragments; Okazaki fragments are a lagging-strand feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. mRNA and anticodons belong to translation, not to DNA replication or Okazaki fragment formation.
explanations.C: Correct. Okazaki fragments are the short DNA pieces produced during discontinuous synthesis of the lagging strand, each starting with its own RNA primer. After DNA polymerase I removes the primers and fills the gaps, DNA ligase forms the phosphodiester bonds that seal the remaining nicks between adjacent fragments, joining them into one continuous strand.
explanations.D: Incorrect. tRNA belongs to translation, not replication, and polymerase extends strands rather than sealing nicks between finished fragments — that final sealing step is ligase's role.

questions.title: Molecule that serves as the DNA replication primer
questions.question: Given that DNA polymerases are unable to synthesize DNA without a primer, what molecule serves as the primer for these enzymes during DNA replication?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A five-carbon sugar alone is not a nucleic acid and provides no base-paired 3'-OH end for a polymerase to extend from.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deoxyribose by itself, without attached bases or phosphates, cannot base-pair with the template strand and so cannot function as a primer.
explanations.C: Correct. Because DNA polymerases can only extend an existing 3'-OH end and cannot start a new chain from scratch, primase first lays down a short RNA molecule that base-pairs with the template. DNA polymerase then extends from this RNA primer's 3' end, and the RNA is later excised and replaced with DNA.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Primers are nucleic acid, not protein; a protein with free hydroxyl groups could not base-pair with the DNA template to be extended in sequence.
